extracted.intended_audience: business leaders, PR and crisis-communication professionals, case study readers
extracted.subtask_description: A brief case-study analysis of Johnson & Johnson's response to the 1982 Tylenol cyanide crisis, highlighting practical crisis-management principles and actions a company can take to protect public safety and restore trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritizing ethics / putting people before profits
rubrics_metrics.description: Make public safety the primary priority rather than protecting short-term profits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Johnson & Johnson made protecting public safety its clear priority, guided by its corporate credo; this included accepting major financial losses to prevent further harm. Example: the company recalled 31 million bottles at an estimated cost of $100M to demonstrate commitment to customer safety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparent communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain open and honest communication with the public, health officials, and the media throughout the crisis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: J&J kept lines of communication open and made repeated public appearances (CEO James Burke appeared on national TV) to explain the situation and reassure consumers. Transparent messaging fosters credibility and helps calm public panic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Swift, decisive action (rapid recall and containment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Act quickly and decisively to remove harmful products or otherwise contain risks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The company initiated a nationwide recall of 31 million bottles shortly after discovering tampering. Speedy action reduces further harm and signals seriousness of response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proactive innovation to prevent recurrence
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the crisis as an opportunity to introduce lasting safety improvements that address root causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: J&J introduced tamper-proof packaging—an industry-first—that became a new safety standard. Turning fixes into industry-leading safeguards helps restore trust and prevents repeat incidents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leadership visibility and direct engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Senior leaders should be visible, take responsibility, and communicate directly with stakeholders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CEO James Burke's numerous television appearances exemplified visible leadership. High-level engagement signals accountability and can reassure consumers and regulators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accepting financial cost to demonstrate responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Be prepared to incur financial losses as part of responsible crisis handling to show commitment to stakeholders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: J&J absorbed an estimated $100M cost for the recall. Willingness to bear costs can be a tangible demonstration of prioritizing safety and ethics over short-term earnings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure outcomes by restored trust and market recovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate success by whether customer trust is rebuilt and market position recovers after the response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Despite temporary share loss, Tylenol regained its top position, recovering 70% of market share within a year—used here as an outcome metric indicating effective crisis management.

rubrics_metrics.name: Values-driven decision making (guided by corporate credo)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let organizational values and formal credos guide decisions during crises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: J&J's actions were guided by its corporate credo emphasizing responsibility to customers and communities. Explicit values can provide decision-making clarity under pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Turning crisis into opportunity for resilience
rubrics_metrics.description: Leverage a crisis to implement changes that strengthen the organization long-term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The case emphasizes transforming setbacks into improvements (e.g., new packaging standards) so organizations can emerge stronger and more resilient after a crisis.
